title: The Molding of Adam and Eve: How the Counterfeit Likeness Carries the Seal of the Revealed Image
arc: The teaching shows how the Third Ambassador's revealed image, sent for the sake of the crucified Son, is seized in counterfeit by the archons who in their lust mold Adam and Eve as a likeness imprinted with the divine seal yet not in truth — and then situates this molding within a sequence of three earlier moldings of corrupt nature, so that the natural man stands as the conjoined product of the Exalted One's icon and the King of Darkness's matter.
reading:
This chapter answers a single question: how is it that the natural man — Adam and Eve — bears the imprint of the divine image and yet is not the divine image in truth? The teacher works through the question in two large movements. First he expounds the molding of Adam and Eve by the archons as a counterfeit fashioned from the revealed icon of the Ambassador. Then he sets that molding alongside three other moldings of corrupt nature, so that the place of humanity in the cosmos is shown precisely.

The first movement begins by insisting that God is intent in heart concerning humanity. The molding of Adam and Eve is no accident of the archons; if the Father had not been intent on humanity, the archons could never have molded humanity according to his likeness, because they would have had nothing to copy. The Third Ambassador, the Lord in his revealing operation, manifests his image forth. The archons and the powers of the cosmos see it, desire it, and fashion forms before that likeness — and these forms are Adam and Eve. They imprint the icon of the Exalted One in the inward heart of their soul and then mold Adam (and Eve) after his likeness. But the teacher is careful: this likeness is in a comparison only, not in truth; it is in the manner of a face that resembles, not the substance.

Why was the image revealed at all, if it could be seized like this? The teacher gives the Ambassador's true purpose: he came not so that the archons of the cosmos might depict his form, but on account of his Son who is crucified in the All — that is, the Living Soul, Divine Truth dispersed and bound in the natural — so that he might raise him, release him forth, redeem him out of the affliction, out of every bond and chain in which the soul is intertwined. The revealing of the image is for the sake of the captive light; the archons' theft of that image is parasitic on the saving operation.

To make this plain, the teaching gives the simile of the noble free woman. She is hidden in her palace, exceedingly wealthy, beautiful, clothed in habits of freedom and ranks of dignity; the fame of her beauty has been scattered into every city, so that the noble ones, the magnates, and the commoners desire her face continually but cannot reach her, since she is hidden. She does not wish to leave her chamber and come into the street to be gazed upon by men; only some necessity draws her out, namely the beloved brother for whose sake alone she will turn her heart toward the watch outside, reveal her face, and uncover her fire. So also the Third Ambassador. He came to manifest his image not to gratify the archons' longing but only because of the necessity of the work — the redemption of the Son crucified in the cosmos. The archons stand in the position of the watching men of the street: they see the face that was not unveiled for them, and they seize what they see.

What follows is the inner mechanism of that seizure. The archons, beholding the desire-arousing and beautiful icon, are inflamed; they mingle in their pleasure with their female counterpart, are stripped bare, and burn in their lust like a man burning for a face of desire. In that very burning they receive the seal of the revealed icon; they are likened to it in a likeness; the imprint stamps itself upon their begetting. The new birth which they then beget in their cosmos — Adam and Eve — is therefore from the beginning a likeness of the Exalted One's image, because no such icon exists in the lower worlds except as derived from above. The natural man is, in his inmost form, an impressed seal of the divine icon; in his outward begetting he is the fruit of archontic concupiscence. He is the meeting-place of these two: an image of the Most High molded by the demiurges of self-love.

The second movement orders this molding within a fourfold series, so that one may see what kind of molding the human is. The teacher distinguishes the moldings that did not come about through manifest intercourse from the molding that did. There is a first molding bound at the boundary of the sea and driven forth from the sphere, where the fire and enthumesis of Hyle mold themselves out of themselves — concupiscence as self-generating principle in the receptive depth. There is a second molding: the Nature that fell upon the earth, whose own enthumesis became to her an image-painter; she molded herself by herself into the very root of Death, rose up out of the sea threatening to destroy the works of Life, and was met at that hour by the Adamas of Light, the great teaching of Maidenhood, who subdued her in the cisterns of the north and set his foot upon her until the end of the cosmos. There is a third molding: the Nature that fell upon the Boastful Tree and stood fixed in him. And then there is the new molding — Adam and Eve — which is brought forth in the cosmos and manifested in it. These three earlier moldings are corruptions in which Hyle generates from herself alone, or falls into earth, or fastens onto the bitter tree; they are pure productions of the corrupt feminine pole. The molding of humanity is different: in substance it shares with these archontic productions and stands under the King of Darkness, but its form has been imprinted with the icon of the Exalted One. It is conjoined — that is its definition. Adam and Eve are the place where the seal of the divine image and the substance of the proprium are joined together, manifested forth in the cosmos.

The whole teaching is thus a doctrine of the natural man as a mingled state. The image of God is genuinely sealed within him, because the Lord's revealing of his image preceded any molding the archons could perform. But the substance into which that seal is pressed is the matter of self-love, fashioned by archontic lust at the moment of seeing the icon. The human is therefore neither a pure work of darkness, like the self-generated moldings of Hyle, nor the truth of the divine image itself; he is the imprinted likeness — true in seal, counterfeit in substance — and this is exactly the state from which the redemption of the crucified Son must proceed. The Ambassador revealed his image for the sake of releasing the captive soul; the archons' theft of that image is what produced the human form that now carries the soul; the teaching holds these two together as the very logic of how regeneration becomes possible.
